phonemes.desc: Alveolar tap [ɾ], as in Spanish 'pero' — the Māori r, light and quick, never the English growl.
Short back rounded vowel [ɔ], pure and unglided, as in British 'pot'.
Velar nasal [ŋ] — the sound of English 'singer', written ng as a single consonant.
Final short [ɔ]; Māori vowels are level, so the name ends as openly as it began.

pronunciation.approximation: 'RAW-ngaw' — tap the r lightly, keep both o's short and pure, and sound the ng as in 'singer'. Stress falls on the first syllable.

kin.label: Proto-Polynesian
kin.form: *longo, 'to hear, news' — the reconstructed root behind every form of the name (Biggs, POLLEX; Tregear, Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary).

kin.label: Hawaiian
kin.form: Lono — god of agriculture, rain, and peace, honoured in the Makahiki festival (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology).

kin.label: Tahitian
kin.form: Ro'o — god of peace and cultivated food (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).

pronunciation.note: Rongo is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Māori spelling carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter that plain ASCII loses — the capital marks a proper name, not a sound. What the restoration keeps is the god's own Polynesian name, unrespelled and unanglicized.

domains.title: Rongo
domains.subtitle: Agriculture
domains.lead: Rongo is the Māori god of cultivated foods and of peace — the kūmara in the ground, the stored harvest, the quiet field. One of the sons of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, he is the brother who hid from the storm inside the Earth and became, in the people's telling, the very food dug from her bosom. Across Polynesia his name resounds as Hawaiian Lono and Tahitian Ro'o: the god of what is planted.

cards.name: The Kūmara
cards.desc: The sweet potato is his body in Māori telling; the first-fruits rites invoke Rongomatāne before a single tuber is lifted.

cards.name: Peace
cards.desc: His name from Proto-Polynesian *longo, 'news, hearing' — the settled season when tidings travel instead of war-parties.

cards.name: The Hidden Brother
cards.desc: Rongo and Haumia thrust themselves into the Earth to escape Tāwhirimātea's storm; the digging-stick and the karakia bring them back as food.

cards.name: The Polynesian Circuit
cards.desc: One god under many names: Rongo in Aotearoa, Lono in Hawai'i, Ro'o in Tahiti — the oldest shared deity of the Pacific.

symbols.name: Kūmara
symbols.meaning: The sweet potato, staple crop of the Māori; Rongo is the kūmara's guardian, and the garden's tapu is his.

symbols.name: The digging-stick (kō)
symbols.meaning: The tool that finds the hidden god; planting with the kō is a ritual approach to Rongo, not mere labour.

symbols.name: The storage pit (rua kūmara)
symbols.meaning: The earth-store where the harvest sleeps safe through winter — the tangible shape of the peace Rongo guards.

symbols.name: The Makahiki images
symbols.meaning: Hawaiian Lono's woven standards, carried around the islands in the season when war is suspended and games begin.

mythology.lead: Rongo stands at the junction of garden and peace. His cycle — born in darkness between Sky and Earth, hidden from the storm, dug up as food — makes cultivation itself a rescue of hidden gods, and the planted field a treaty renewed every spring.

myths.title: A Son Between Sky and Earth
myths.text: In the Māori creation told by Wiremu Maihi Te Rangikāheke and printed by George Grey, the Sky Father Ranginui and the Earth Mother Papatūānuku lay locked in an embrace, and their children — among them Rongo, Tāne, Tangaroa, Haumia-tiketike, Tāwhirimātea, and Tūmatauenga — lived crushed in darkness between them. Rongo's fiercest brother Tū urged the final solution: kill the parents and have done. The others recoiled at the thought of slaying their own father and mother, and the gentler plan of Tāne prevailed — the parents would be forced apart, not slain. Rongo stood with Tāne's party. Tāne braced his head against the earth and his feet against the sky and thrust, and light came pouring in where darkness had been (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, the legend of the children of Rangi and Papa). In this telling the gods of food are born of suffocation: Rongo's whole mythology begins in a space too tight to live in, and every field he blesses is a little of that darkness opened to the sun.

myths.title: Hidden in the Bosom of the Earth
myths.text: Tāwhirimātea, god of winds, had opposed the separation of his parents, and when it was done he took war to his brothers. Tangaroa fled to the sea; Tāne withdrew into the forests; but Rongo and Haumia-tiketike thrust themselves into the open bosom of their mother the Earth, and there they hid (Grey, Polynesian Mythology). When the storm at last spent itself, it was Tūmatauenga, the one brother who had stood his ground, who turned on the hidden gods: he dug with a sharp stake into the earth and dragged them out — Rongo's kūmara and Haumia's aruhe, the fern-root — and so those foods were given to humankind. The myth is exact about its meaning: agriculture is not a theft from nature but a rescue of hidden gods. The digging-stick wounds the mother gently, and what it brings up is a brother.

myths.title: The First Fruits of Rongomatāne
myths.text: In ritual rather than epic, Rongo's story was re-enacted every planting season. The fuller name Rongomatāne — Rongo-of-the-abundant-soil — was invoked in the karakia that opened the kūmara garden; the seed-tubers went into the ground with the digging-stick, the first fruits of the old crop were returned to the god before anyone ate, and the storehouse stood under his tapu until the new year (Tregear, The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary, s.v. Rongo; Best, Māori Religion and Mythology). To eat kūmara without acknowledging Rongo was to break the treaty between the digger and the hidden brother; Best records planting prayers that address the god by name and lineage, asking the earth's permission as one asks a chief's. The myth's ending was thus rewritten annually in every garden of the North Island: the god hides in the ground, the people dig him up with thanks, and the harvest is the two keeping faith.

myths.title: Lono of Hawai'i and the Season of Peace
myths.text: In Hawai'i the same god walks as Lono, lord of agriculture, rain, and peace, whose annual Makahiki season suspended war, gathered the year's tribute on a circuit of the islands, and filled the days with games, feasting, and sport (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology). When Captain Cook anchored at Kealakekua Bay in November 1778 — in the heart of Makahiki — the Hawaiians received him as the god's own return from Kahiki, his ancestral land; the identification held for weeks before it collapsed in violence (Sahlins, Islands of History; the sceptical counter-case is Obeyesekere, The Apotheosis of Captain Cook). Whatever the truth of that reception, the scholarship agrees on the god: a deity whose season stops wars and feeds the people, met on his own festival ground. Rongo's pan-Polynesian career — kūmara-god in the south, peace-king in the north — makes him one of the deepest layers of shared Oceanic religion.

lore.syncretism: Rongo is one half of the oldest Polynesian pairing: the agriculture-god beside the sea-god Tangaroa. From Aotearoa to Hawai'i his name barely changes — Māori Rongo, Hawaiian Lono, Tahitian Ro'o, Cook Islands Rongo — a stability that marks him as a first-generation deity carried in the great voyaging canoes (Tregear; Beckwith; Henry, Ancient Tahiti). In Mangaia, strikingly, Rongo is the paramount god of war as well as of the cultivated field — the inversion shows the two faces of the planted life, which must be defended as well as tended. The Hawaiians pressed him furthest: Lono's Makahiki circuit made him a visiting king whose arrival ends warfare, and the eighteenth-century encounter with Cook turned the old theology into world history. Christian missionaries suppressed the cult, but the name survived in whakataukī, in the school calendars of the Hawaiian Renaissance, and in the revived Makahiki itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: Rongo's legacy is a foodway. The kūmara — a tropical plant coaxed to fruit in temperate Aotearoa — remains the emblem of Māori horticulture, and the storage pits that held it still pock the volcanic fields around Tāmaki Makaurau. In Hawai'i the Makahiki has been publicly revived since the 1970s, with canoes and schoolchildren carrying Lono's images round the coast as of old. Rongo endures as a given name across Polynesia, and the scholarship built on Grey, Tregear, and Beckwith keeps his cycle — separation, storm, hiding, harvest — the standard account of how the Pacific's peoples explain their bread. Few gods live so quietly and so persistently: in the ground, in the storehouse, in the season of peace.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Rongo is the god of the planted world, and his theology is a parable of gentle extraction. He does not demand conquest or ecstasy; he asks that the earth be opened carefully, that the first fruits be returned, that peace hold while the crop ripens. In an age that treats food as logistics, Rongo remembers that eating is a relationship — between the digger and the hidden god, between the season of war and the season of the storehouse.

His pan-Polynesian name is itself a map of voyaging: wherever the canoes landed, Rongo landed with them, taking local form but keeping his office. That a whole ocean could agree on one quiet god of the garden says something the loud gods never manage: the things that feed us are the things we hold most in common.
lore.archaeology: Rongo leaves no temples — Polynesian religion built few — but his archive is underfoot. Thousands of rua kūmara (storage pits), dug into the volcanic soils of the Auckland region and preserved by the geochemistry that protected the crop, survive from the fourteenth century onward and mark the god's territory field by field. In Hawai'i the heiau platforms dedicated to Lono survive along the Kona coast, among them Hikiau Heiau above Kealakekua Bay, beside which Cook's party recorded the Makahiki rites in 1779; its stone terraces still overlook the water. The digging-stick itself, the kō, survives in museum collections — a plain agricultural tool whose every use was once prayer.
